newsitem.title: USA: Los Angeles mayor wins second term in office.
newsitem.headline: Los Angeles mayor wins second term in office.

text.p: Los Angeles Mayor Richard Riordan handily won re-election as the leader of the second-largest city in the United States late on Tuesday, with an estimated 60 percent of the vote.

"Los Angeles deserves to be proud ... Los Angeles is back," Riordan declared in his victory speech, referring to setbacks the city has overcome, including the 1992 riots, the recession and the 1994 earthquake.
With nearly 20 percent of the votes counted at 11 p.m. PDT (2 a.m. EDT) Riordan had 60 percent of the votes over opponent Tom Hayden's 35 percent.
Hayden, a former activist who represents Los Angeles in the California state Senate, told supporters he still believed in his dream of making Los Angeles a more desirable city to live in.
"Whatever the outcome is tonight, we have to continue that dream, because without that dream we are not human beings," he said.
He added that he had tried to contact Riordan at the hotel where the mayor was celebrating his victory, but had been unable to get through to him.
Despite a spirited election campaign, voter turnout was one of the lowest ever for a mayoral election in the city, with less that 30 percent of the electorate going to the polls.

Although Riordan -- a wealthy businessman who accepts a salary of only $1 a year as mayor and who was first elected in 1993 -- is a Republican and Hayden a Democrat, the race was non-partisan with neither candidate running under his party banner.
Indeed, Riordan had the backing of several prominent local Democrats while there were a number of Republicans in Hayden's camp.

Hayden, who was once married to actress Jane Fonda when both were anti-Vietnam War activists, injected the only real note of acrimony into the campaign when he accused Riordan of being a "racist" -- a remark he quickly withdrew.
Hayden is a former head of the militant Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), and was part of the famous Chicago Seven trial of war protesters.
In other races, James Hahn appeared headed for a fourth term as Los Angeles city attorney, beating San Fernando Valley attorney Ted Stein by a margin of 61 percent to 38 percent.

Voters appeared to favor an initiative to rewrite the city's 72-year-old charter, which was winning by 60 percent to 39 percent, and another that would raise $2.4 billion to repair and renovate aging city schools, which was favored by 70 percent of voters to 29 percent who opposed the measure.
